content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the principles of green chemistry
Explain how green chemistry reduces environmental impact
Give examples of green chemistry in practice
Evaluate chemical processes in terms of sustainability

(also called sustainable chemistry) is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances. It aims to prevent pollution at source rather than treating it afterwards.
Designing chemicals and processes to reduce environmental impact
Prevention of pollution at the source
Considers entire life cycle of chemicals
Designing processes that don't create pollution
Using safer chemicals from the start
Preventing problems rather than solving them
Prevent waste rather than treat it
Design products to be less toxic
Use catalysts instead of stoichiometric reagents
It's better to prevent waste than clean it up
"An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure"
$$\text{Atom economy} = \frac{\text{M}_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{Sum of M}_r \text{ of all reactants}} \times 100\%$$
Has properties of liquid and gas
Used for decaffeinating coffee, dry cleaning
What percentage of atoms become product?
What are the risks of accidents?

All atoms from reactants end up in the product
This is excellent from a green chemistry perspective
Explain why using a catalyst is a principle of green chemistry.
Catalysts are not consumed (used in small amounts)
The Haber process uses an iron catalyst to produce ammonia at lower temperatures than would otherwise be possible.
Compare the sustainability of making ethanol by fermentation versus hydration of ethene.
By-product: CO₂ (but absorbed by growing plants)
Fermentation is more sustainable despite lower atom economy because it uses renewable resources and is carbon neutral.
Thinking green chemistry is just about recycling
It's about designing processes to prevent pollution in the first place
Assuming higher atom economy is always greener
Must consider energy, toxicity, feedstock too
Thinking catalysts are consumed in reactions
Catalysts are regenerated and used in small amounts
